newsitem.title: ITALY: Too early to talk of strike on welfare-Italy union.
newsitem.headline: Too early to talk of strike on welfare-Italy union.

text.p: The head of Italy's biggest labour group said on Thursday it was too early to talk of striking over plans to reform the welfare state, but said that, if the government did not adopt common positions, action may be inevitable.
"It's a question we're not posing at the moment," CGIL leader Sergio Cofferati told state broadcaster RAI, referring to the possibility of breaking off the talks, or calling a strike.

Prime Minister Romano Prodi on Wednesday opened talks with the leaders of Italy's three main union confederations, trade bodies and employers' group Confindustria on the thorny question of reforms of the welfare state and generous pension system.
Prodi presented a document that Cofferati immediately dismissed as wholly inadequate. Union leaders want talks to proceed on the basis of a document they have drawn up.

"If the governmnet is not flexible and puts forward proposals which are not shared, the talks will be broken off," Cofferati said. "Then the government will decide what to do and we will behave accordingly."

Cabinet undersecretary Enrico Micheli told private TV station TeleMonteCarlo that the talks, which are expected to last all summer, should examine the "inbalances which still exist" after a partial pension reform carried out in 1995.
"There's no doubt, we have to start from there," he said.

Italy is under pressure to carry out a convincing reform of social spending -- and to shake up its pensions system -- to prove that public finances will be kept under control before the planned 1999 launch of the single European currency.

The Prodi document called for a review of a generous early retirement system that allows Italians to draw a pension based on the length of service rather than because they have reached retirement age, questioning whether the country could afford it.
